method: basE91 is Joachim Henke's binary-to-text encoding: 91 printable characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and 29 punctuation marks, including the double quote and excluding the space, the single quote and the backslash) carry 13 or 14 bits at a time. The encoder keeps a bit queue in an integer. Each input byte is appended at the queue's current bit offset in little-endian bit order, and once 14 or more bits are queued it reads the low 13 bits; when that value is 88 or less the 13-bit reading is unambiguous, so 13 bits are consumed, otherwise the low 14 bits are read and 14 are consumed. The value is written as two characters, least-significant digit first: value modulo 91 and value divided by 91. When the input ends, the leftover 1 to 16 bits are written as one character, plus a second character when more than 7 bits remain or the leftover value exceeds 90, so no padding characters exist. Decoding mirrors the process: each pair of alphabet characters forms value = first + 91 * second, its width is 13 bits when value AND 8191 is 88 or less and 14 bits otherwise, and the queue is drained one byte at a time while more than 7 bits remain; a final unpaired character contributes one last byte. Because the scheme is a continuous bit queue rather than fixed frames, the overhead is data dependent: at most 23% and as little as 14%, against 33% for Base64. Characters outside the alphabet are ignored by the decoder, which is how a line-wrapped payload still decodes; the page counts and reports them. Input text is encoded as UTF-8 with lone surrogates replaced by U+FFFD, and hex mode reads pairs of hexadecimal digits as bytes so binary data can be encoded. Decoded bytes are shown as UTF-8 text when they form valid sequences and as uppercase hexadecimal otherwise, and the decoder rejects truncated, overlong, surrogate and out-of-range sequences instead of substituting replacement characters. Input is limited to 100,000 characters, the arithmetic is plain integer work with no clock, storage, network or third-party library, and the encoding is not encryption.

sources.title: basE91 — an advanced method for encoding binary data as ASCII characters (Joachim Henke): its overhead is at most 23% and can range down to 14%, against 33% for base64
Henke's basE91 reference implementation (base91.c): the 91-character encode table, the 13/14-bit queue shared by encoder and decoder, the trailing-bit rules and the decoder's 91-value ignore table
